extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigates the relationship between acute plasma total tau levels and prolonged return to play (RTP) after sport-related concussion (SRC) in collegiate athletes. It found that elevated plasma tau concentrations, particularly within 6, 24, and 72 hours post-SRC, are significantly associated with a prolonged RTP (>10 days). Furthermore, baseline tau levels were higher in athletes (concussed and non-concussed) compared to non-athlete controls, and physical exertion itself can independently elevate tau.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study focuses on single sport-related concussion events in collegiate contact sport athletes and the impact of physical exertion. Blood samples were collected at baseline (pre-season) and at multiple time points post-SRC (6, 24, 48, 72 hours, and 7 days). Return to Play (RTP) durations varied (2 to 263 days) and were categorized into short (<=10 days) and long (>10 days) groups for comparison. While no specific 'dose' or severity of concussion was quantified, the study compared temporal responses of tau and noted that physical exertion, such as exercise or boxing bouts, can independently cause transient tau elevation.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level (measured by ultrasensitive immunoassay / Simoa method)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Higher in athletes at baseline compared to non-athletes; higher post-SRC in athletes with prolonged RTP (especially at 6, 24, 72 hours); lower in SRC athletes at 24 and 72 hours compared to athlete controls still playing; transiently higher after physical exertion.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher mean tau concentrations in both athlete groups (concussed and controls) compared to non-athlete healthy controls at baseline and all other time points (F 101,2 = 19.644, p < 0.01). In SRC athletes, those with long RTP had higher tau concentrations overall compared to short RTP athletes (F 39,1 = 3.59, p = 0.022), specifically at 6 hours (10.98 vs 7.02 pg/mL, p = 0.02), 24 hours (7.19 vs 4.08 pg/mL, p < 0.01), and 72 hours (6.29 vs 3.94 pg/mL, p < 0.01) post-SRC. At 6 hours post-SRC, long RTP athletes showed a mean increase of 2.26 pg/mL from baseline (F 33,1 = 5.09, p < 0.01), while short RTP athletes showed a mean reduction of 1.19 pg/mL. SRC athletes also had significantly lower mean total tau at 24 hours (6.06 vs 7.89 pg/mL, p = 0.030) and 72 hours (5.19 vs 6.94 pg/mL, p = 0.041) post-SRC compared to athlete controls. Elevated tau levels were also observed 1-6 days post-boxing bouts (without concussion) and 1 hour after exercise in non-concussed athletes.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of neuronal injury and damage, axonal damage following traumatic brain injury, blood-brain barrier permeability changes, and is a hallmark pathologic feature in chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) due to accumulation of phosphorylated tau and neurofibrillary tangles.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Acute phase following sport-related concussion (SRC) in collegiate contact sport athletes, differentiating between short and prolonged return-to-play (RTP) durations. Also relevant in the context of physical exertion, exercise, subconcussive blows, and repetitive mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) without sufficient recovery.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher acute plasma total tau levels (especially within 6, 24, and 72 hours post-SRC) are significant predictors of prolonged Return to Play (RTP >10 days) after sport-related concussion, with predictive accuracy (e.g., AUC 0.81 at 6 hours, AUC 0.82 at 72 hours). It serves as a prognostic indicator for recovery duration, helps inform RTP decisions, mitigates risks of premature return, and indicates the severity of neuronal injury. Elevated tau is also linked to changes in cognitive performance, balance, and long-term chronic neuronal pathology such as CTE.
